newsitem.title: INDIA: India, S.Africa to seek U.N., Commonwealth reforms.
newsitem.headline: India, S.Africa to seek U.N., Commonwealth reforms.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela, beginning a three-day visit to India, said on Thursday the two nations would sign a joint declaration seeking democratic reforms in the United Nations and the Commonwealth.
"Firstly, we will be signing what we call a Delhi Declaration of intentions," Mandela told reporters after a ceremonial reception at New Delhi's presidential palace.
He said India and South Africa were keen to restructure the United Nations and would hold talks during his visit on the issue.
Mandela said they would also address common concerns on the Commonwealth grouping and the Non-Aligned Movement of developing countries that oppose alignment to any superpower.

"We don't accept that a few nations should have the right to prevent or undermine what the international community decides. I believe that the republic of India and South Africa are unanimous in that view," he said.

Mandela did not elaborate, but was apparently referring to veto powers for some nations on the United Nations' Security Council, which has faced criticism from developing countries for overruling the larger General Assembly.
India has been lobbying for a permanent seat on the Security Council and has found support from several developing countries.
Mandela said the two nations were keen on promoting democracy in Commonwealth nations, once ruled by Britain.

"The Commonwealth is faced also with a number of problems where there are countries which still practise one-party states, where there are no popular structures at all," Mandela said without elaborating.
